question: What is idempotency in REST APIs and why does it matter?
title: Idempotency in REST APIs
direct_answer: Idempotency means making the same API call multiple times produces the same result as making it once. It matters for retry safety — if a network failure occurs, it's safe to retry idempotent calls without creating duplicate side effects.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding distributed systems challenges in REST API design
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking idempotency just means same response — it means same system state after multiple calls
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the real problem: network timeout doesn't tell you if the server received the request

sections.title: Why Idempotency Matters
sections.content: In distributed systems, network calls can fail at any point. If a DELETE request times out, did the server receive it? If you retry, will deleting twice cause issues? For idempotent operations, retrying is safe because the end state is the same. For non-idempotent POST (create order), retrying could create two orders and charge the customer twice.

sections.title: Idempotency in Practice
content: GET, PUT, DELETE: naturally idempotent by HTTP spec
POST: not idempotent by default — need special handling
DELETE idempotency: first call removes resource (200), second gets 404 — same end state (no resource)
PUT idempotency: calling PUT /users/1 {name: 'Alice'} 100 times → always {name: 'Alice'}
POST idempotency via Idempotency-Key header: payment APIs (Stripe)
Optimistic locking: version field prevents duplicate updates
Unique constraint: database prevents duplicate records

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: Idempotency means calling an operation multiple times has the same effect as calling it once. This is critical when network calls fail — you don't know if the server got the request, so you might retry. GET and DELETE are naturally idempotent — retrying a delete still leaves no resource. PUT is idempotent — putting the same data repeatedly doesn't change anything. POST is the problem child — creating an order twice charges twice. Payment systems like Stripe solve this with an Idempotency-Key header: you send a unique key per logical operation, and the server returns the same response for repeated requests with the same key.

seo.metaTitle: API Idempotency Explained | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn idempotency in REST APIs, retry safety, and Idempotency-Key pattern. Java fresher prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: Idempotent means calling the same endpoint multiple times is as safe as calling it once — critical when networks drop and you have to retry.

beats.text: Idempotency means the end state of the system is the same whether you called the operation once or a hundred times. It's not about getting the same HTTP response code — it's about the server-side state being identical regardless of how many times the request arrived.

Networks fail in ways that leave you uncertain. A timeout doesn't tell you if the server received the request before dropping the connection. If you retry a non-idempotent operation like 'create order', you might charge the customer twice. Idempotency gives you the freedom to retry without fear.

items: GET: naturally idempotent — reading a todo 100 times leaves 100 identical copies in your client, zero change on the server
PUT: idempotent — replacing todo 42 with title done 100 times still leaves todo 42 with title done
DELETE: idempotent — first call deletes and returns 200; second call gets 404, but the end state (todo gone) is the same
POST: not idempotent by default — POST /todos 10 times creates 10 todos

beats.text: Mobile user taps Pay. Network is slow. App retries after 3 seconds. Without idempotency, two payments go through. With an Idempotency-Key header (a UUID the client generates per logical operation), the server recognises the retry and returns the original response without processing a second time. Stripe uses exactly this pattern. candidates miss: idempotency is about system state, not HTTP response codes. DELETE returning 404 on the second call is still idempotent — the resource is gone either way.

items: Thinking idempotency means same response code — it means same end state; DELETE returning 404 on retry is still idempotent
Assuming you never need to retry — network timeouts are common; non-idempotent retries create silent duplicates

speakable_v2.cap: Idempotent = safe to retry. GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent. POST is not — use Idempotency-Key pattern when you need POST to be retry-safe.

question: How do you implement idempotency for POST requests in Spring Boot?
title: POST Idempotency in Spring Boot
direct_answer: Implement idempotency for POST using an Idempotency-Key header. Store the key and response in a cache/database. On duplicate requests, return the cached response. Database unique constraints also prevent duplicate records.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to solve real distributed systems problems in Spring Boot
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing a concrete implementation pattern
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the complete pattern: Redis cache for idempotency store, interceptor for reuse

sections.title: Idempotency Key Pattern
sections.content: The Idempotency-Key pattern: client generates a unique UUID per operation. Server checks if this key exists in its store (Redis or DB). If yes, return the stored response. If no, execute and store the result. This makes POST as safe to retry as GET.

sections.title: Implementation Steps
content: Client sends: POST /orders, header: Idempotency-Key: uuid-1234
Server checks Redis/DB for key uuid-1234
Key found: return cached response (409 Conflict or stored 201 response)
Key not found: process request, store response with key, set TTL
Database unique constraint as fallback for critical operations
Spring Boot interceptor or AOP aspect to handle key checking centrally
Key TTL: typically 24 hours to 7 days depending on use case

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: The standard approach is an Idempotency-Key header pattern. The client generates a UUID for each logical operation and sends it as a header. The server, before processing, checks if it's seen this key before — usually in Redis with a TTL. If the key exists, return the previous response immediately. If not, process and store the result. For payment flows, I'd add a database unique constraint on order reference numbers as a hard safety net. In Spring Boot, I'd build this as a HandlerInterceptor or AOP aspect so every POST endpoint gets idempotency support without duplicating the logic.

seo.metaTitle: POST Idempotency Spring Boot | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Implement POST idempotency with Idempotency-Key header in Spring Boot. Java backend prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: POST is not idempotent by default — the Idempotency-Key pattern makes it retry-safe without changing the endpoint itself.

beats.text: The Idempotency-Key pattern works like this: the client generates a unique UUID per logical operation and sends it as an Idempotency-Key request header. The server checks whether it has seen that key before. If yes, it returns the stored response. If no, it processes the request and stores the result before responding.

HTTP POST has no built-in retry safety. Rather than changing how POST works, the pattern adds a side-channel key that the server uses to detect duplicates. The client controls uniqueness — one key per logical action, regardless of how many HTTP requests it takes to complete it.

items: Client generates UUID Idempotency-Key once per operation — retries reuse the same key
Server checks Redis: key exists means duplicate, return cached response immediately
Key not found: process request, write result to Redis with TTL (24h typical), then respond
Database unique constraint on idempotency key as hard fallback — catches Redis cache evictions
HandlerInterceptor or AOP aspect centralises key-check logic so every POST gets it for free

beats.text: Payment flow: client sends POST /payments with header Idempotency-Key: uuid-abc. Server runs SETNX uuid-abc in Redis — succeeds, so it processes the payment and stores {status: 201, paymentId: 55} under that key. Network drops. Client retries with the same key. SETNX fails — key exists. Server returns the stored response without charging again. sharp edge: two simultaneous requests with the same key create a race condition. The fix is acquiring a distributed lock on the key before the check — SETNX with a short TTL works as a lock here.

items: Only handling the happy path — concurrent duplicates need a distributed lock to prevent two threads both seeing a missing key and both processing
Setting the TTL too short — if the client retries after the key expires, you process it again; 24 hours is a safe minimum for payments

speakable_v2.cap: Idempotency-Key = client UUID per operation + Redis store + optional DB constraint. Three layers cover single retries, concurrent duplicates, and cache evictions.

question: What is the difference between idempotency and safety in HTTP?
title: Idempotency vs Safety
direct_answer: Safety means an operation has no side effects — it doesn't change server state (GET, HEAD). Idempotency means repeating the operation produces the same result. All safe methods are idempotent, but not all idempotent methods are safe.

interviewer_intent.testing: Precise HTTP knowledge showing maturity beyond basic usage
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating safe and idempotent as synonyms
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give the concrete example: DELETE is idempotent but not safe

sections.title: Safe vs Idempotent
sections.content: These are two separate properties. Safety is about side effects — does calling this operation change anything? Idempotency is about repeating — does calling it again change anything? GET is both: no side effects, same result every time. DELETE is idempotent (result is same — no resource) but not safe (it changes state the first time).

sections.title: Method Properties Matrix
content: GET: safe ✓, idempotent ✓
HEAD: safe ✓, idempotent ✓
OPTIONS: safe ✓, idempotent ✓
PUT: safe ✗, idempotent ✓
DELETE: safe ✗, idempotent ✓
PATCH: safe ✗, idempotent ✓ (when implemented correctly)
POST: safe ✗, idempotent ✗
Safe means read-only from server state perspective

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: Safety and idempotency are distinct properties. Safety means the operation doesn't change server state — GET is safe, you're just reading. Idempotency means repeating the operation gives the same outcome. DELETE is idempotent but not safe: the first call deletes the resource (state change), but calling it again still leaves no resource — same end state. POST is neither safe nor idempotent — it creates a resource and calling it twice creates two. PUT is idempotent but not safe — it modifies state, but doing it 100 times with the same data always results in the same state.

seo.metaTitle: HTTP Safety vs Idempotency | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Understand the difference between safe and idempotent HTTP methods. Java fresher interview prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: Safe and idempotent sound similar but they're not synonyms — DELETE is a clear example of the difference.

groups.label: Safe
groups.text: A method is safe if it doesn't modify server state at all. GET and HEAD are safe — they only read. Calling them leaves the world exactly as it was.

groups.label: Idempotent
groups.text: A method is idempotent if calling it multiple times produces the same end state as calling it once. It may change state — it just doesn't keep changing it on repeats.

items: Use the safe distinction when reasoning about caching or browser prefetch — only safe methods should be cached or auto-followed
Use the idempotent distinction when reasoning about retries — only idempotent operations are safe to retry without extra key management

beats.text: DELETE /todos/42 is idempotent because calling it twice still leaves no todo 42. But it's not safe — the first call deletes the resource, which is definitely a state change. GET /todos is both: no state change and same result every call. non-obvious: all safe methods are idempotent (a pure read repeated is a pure read), but the reverse is not true — DELETE changes state the first time, so it's not safe.

speakable_v2.cap: Safe = no state change at all (GET, HEAD). Idempotent = same end state after repeats (GET, PUT, DELETE). Every safe method is idempotent but not vice versa.

question: How does optimistic locking relate to idempotency in Spring Boot?
title: Optimistic Locking and Idempotency
direct_answer: Optimistic locking uses a version field to detect concurrent modifications. While not the same as idempotency, it prevents the lost update problem — two concurrent PUTs don't silently overwrite each other. Use @Version in JPA entities for optimistic locking.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of concurrency in REST APIs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing optimistic locking with idempotency — they solve different problems
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the lost update problem and how @Version prevents it

sections.title: The Lost Update Problem
sections.content: Without concurrency control, two clients can read a resource simultaneously, modify it independently, and write back — the second write silently overwrites the first. This is the lost update problem. Optimistic locking uses a version number: you must include the current version in your update request; if someone else updated first, you get an error.

sections.title: Optimistic Locking in Spring/JPA
content: @Version on Long/Integer field in entity: JPA auto-increments on each update
PUT /users/1 {name: 'Alice', version: 5} → JPA checks version matches
If version mismatch: OptimisticLockException → return 409 Conflict
Client must retry with latest version
ETag header: HTTP standard way to implement optimistic locking in REST
ETag response: ETag: '5', client sends: If-Match: '5' with PUT
Idempotency key prevents duplicate creates; optimistic locking prevents duplicate updates

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: Optimistic locking and idempotency solve different problems. Idempotency handles retries — making the same request twice is safe. Optimistic locking handles concurrent updates — two users editing the same record simultaneously. In JPA, I add @Version to an entity field. When updating, JPA checks if the version in the database matches the version in the request. If they don't match, another update happened in between, and JPA throws OptimisticLockException, which I return as 409 Conflict. The HTTP standard way to implement this is ETags — the server returns an ETag header, and the client sends If-Match on updates.

seo.metaTitle: Optimistic Locking JPA Spring Boot | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn optimistic locking with @Version in JPA Spring Boot. Java backend fresher interview prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: Optimistic locking is not the same as idempotency — but they're often confused. One handles concurrent edits, the other handles retries.

beats.text: Optimistic locking prevents the lost update problem — two clients reading and updating the same record simultaneously, where the second write silently overwrites the first. It uses a version field: you must include the current version in your update; if someone else updated first, the server rejects your write.

Without concurrency control, two users editing the same todo simultaneously will lose one person's changes. Optimistic locking is lightweight — no database row lock held between read and write — it just checks the version at write time and fails fast if there's a conflict.

items: @Version on a Long field in the JPA entity — JPA increments it automatically on every update
Client reads entity with version:5, modifies it, sends PUT with version:5
JPA's UPDATE adds WHERE version=5 — if another update already bumped it to 6, zero rows update and OptimisticLockException is thrown
REST convention: return 409 Conflict when OptimisticLockException is caught in @ControllerAdvice
ETag header: HTTP standard for the same idea — server sends ETag: 5, client sends If-Match: 5 with PUT

beats.text: Todo app: two users open todo 42 (version:3) at the same time. User A saves first — version becomes 4. User B saves with version:3 — JPA finds version 4 in DB, throws OptimisticLockException, the controller returns 409. User B reloads, gets version:4, makes their edit, saves successfully. In Spring Boot: add @Version private Long version to your entity. @ControllerAdvice catches OptimisticLockException and returns ResponseEntity with 409. production trap: people confuse this with idempotency. Idempotency handles retry of the same request from one client. Optimistic locking handles concurrent edits from different clients.

items: Confusing optimistic locking with idempotency — optimistic locking is about concurrent edits, idempotency is about safe retries
Not returning 409 for OptimisticLockException — if the client doesn't know there was a conflict, they'll overwrite data silently on retry

speakable_v2.cap: @Version + JPA = optimistic locking. Version mismatch = 409 Conflict. It handles concurrent edits. Idempotency-Key handles retries. Different problems, different solutions.

question: How would you design an idempotent payment API endpoint?
title: Idempotent Payment API Design
direct_answer: Use a client-generated Idempotency-Key header. Store the key with the result in Redis with TTL. On duplicate requests, return the stored response. Add database unique constraint on payment reference. Handle in-progress state with a distributed lock.

interviewer_intent.testing: System design thinking and ability to design for reliability
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Solving only the happy path without considering concurrent requests with same key
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Address the race condition: two simultaneous requests with same idempotency key

sections.title: Payment Idempotency Design
sections.content: Payment APIs are where idempotency matters most — duplicate charges destroy trust. The design must handle: single retries, concurrent duplicate requests, and partial failures (payment processed but response lost).

sections.title: Complete Design
content: Client generates UUID Idempotency-Key for each payment intent
Server: acquire distributed lock on idempotency key (Redis SETNX)
Check if key exists in cache: yes → return cached response
Process payment, store result in Redis with key, set 24h TTL
Release lock
DB: unique constraint on (customer_id, idempotency_key)
Race condition: if two threads acquire lock, second finds result in cache
Partial failure: idempotency key stored before payment, but payment may need retry logic

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: For a payment API, I'd implement full idempotency with three layers. First, the Idempotency-Key header — client sends a UUID per payment attempt. Second, a Redis store: before processing, I try to set a Redis key with SETNX — if it exists, return the cached response. If not, process and store result with 24-hour TTL. Third, a database unique constraint on the idempotency key as a hard safety net. The tricky part is concurrent requests with the same key — I use a distributed lock on the key to ensure only one processes. This is essentially what Stripe does.

followup_questions: How do you handle the case where payment succeeded but the response was lost?

seo.metaTitle: Idempotent Payment API Design | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Design an idempotent payment API with Idempotency-Key and Redis. Java backend fresher prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: A payment endpoint that can charge twice on retry is a trust-destroying bug — idempotency design is how you prevent it.

beats.text: An idempotent payment API must guarantee that a duplicate request — from a retry, a double-tap, or a network replay — results in exactly one charge. The design has three layers: an Idempotency-Key header, a Redis store, and a database unique constraint as a hard fallback.

Payment failures are expensive in both money and trust. A user whose card is charged twice will dispute the transaction and may never return. Building idempotency into the payment endpoint means retries are always safe, regardless of what failed and when.

items: Client generates UUID Idempotency-Key once per payment intent — retries reuse the same key
Server uses Redis SETNX to acquire a lock on the key — ensures only one request processes at a time
If key already exists in Redis: return stored response (the original 201 or error) without charging again
If key is new: process payment, persist result, store response in Redis with 24h TTL, release lock
Database unique constraint on (customer_id, idempotency_key) as hard fallback if Redis is down or TTL expired

beats.text: Scenario: mobile app sends POST /payments with Idempotency-Key: pay-uuid-1. Server acquires Redis lock, processes charge, stores {paymentId:99, status: SUCCESS} under pay-uuid-1, releases lock. Network drops before response. App retries with same key. Server tries SETNX — lock acquired. Checks store — key exists, returns cached {paymentId:99, status: SUCCESS}. One charge. In Spring Boot, a HandlerInterceptor reads the Idempotency-Key header, checks Redis, and either short-circuits with the cached response or lets the request through and stores the response after the controller returns. non-obvious: the race condition case — two simultaneous requests with the same key. SETNX on the key as a mutex means only one proceeds. The second waits briefly, then sees the result in the cache.

items: Only storing the key after success — if the payment succeeds but your Redis write fails, the next retry has no key and charges again; store the key before processing or use a transaction
Not handling concurrent identical requests — without a distributed lock on the key, two simultaneous requests can both see the key missing and both charge

speakable_v2.cap: Three-layer idempotent payment: Idempotency-Key header + Redis store (SETNX lock) + DB unique constraint. Cover single retries, concurrent dupes, and cache eviction.
